title: Loss of GPR75 protects against non-alcoholic fatty liver disease and body fat accumulation
authors: Jia Neng Wee, Sonia M. Grønbech, Jingyi Jessica Li, Yun Li, Buhm Han
abstract: Approximately 1 in 4 people worldwide have non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD); however, there are currently no medications to treat this condition. This study investigated the role of adiposity-associated orphan G protein-coupled receptor 75 (GPR75) in liver lipid accumulation. We profiled Gpr75 expression and report that it is most abundant in the brain. Next, we generated the first single-cell-level analysis of Gpr75 and identified a subpopulation co-expressed with key appetite-regulating hypothalamic neurons. CRISPR-Cas9-deleted Gpr75 mice fed a palatable western diet high in fat adjusted caloric intake to remain in energy balance, thereby preventing NAFLD. Consistent with mouse results, analysis of whole-exome sequencing data from 428,719 individuals (UK Biobank) revealed that variants in GPR75 are associated with a reduced likelihood of hepatic steatosis. Here, we provide a significant advance in understanding of the expression and function of GPR75, demonstrating that it is a promising pharmaceutical target for NAFLD treatment.
text: Huanlongbing (HLB) or greening disease is caused by a vector-transmitted bacteria (Candidatus Liberibacter) leading to severe economic losses to the citrus industry around the world [4]. Most commercial citrus are known to be susceptible to HLB [5]. However, C. australis and other Australian native lime species including Citrus australasica, Citrus glauca and Citrus inodora and their derived hybrids have shown different degrees of resistance to HLB, providing highly valuable genetic resources in breeding HLB resistant cultivars, and for use as rootstocks or interstocks [6]. Recently, a novel class of small antimicrobial peptides (SAMPs) were isolated from C. australasica and other close relatives which can suppress the growth of HLB causing bacteria and promote host immunity in citrus [7]. However, SAMPs have not yet been identified.

title: Mice Lacking Gpr75 are Hypophagic and Thin
authors: David R Powell, Deon D Doree, Christopher M DaCosta, 1 Kenneth A Platt, Robert Brommage, Lindsey Buhring, Jean-Pierre Revelli, and Melanie K Shadoan
abstract: Humans with haploinsufficiency of GPR75, an orphan GPCR, are thin. Gpr75 knockout (KO) mice are also thin with improved glucose homeostasis. We wanted to confirm these findings in Gpr75 KO mice and determine whether decreased energy intake and/or increased energy expenditure contributed to the thin phenotype.
text: Gpr75 KO mice were generated by homologous recombination. All studies compared female and male Gpr75 KO mice to their wild type (WT) littermates. Body composition was measured by DXA and QMR technologies. Glucose homeostasis was evaluated by measuring glucose and insulin levels during oral glucose tolerance tests (OGTTs). Food intake was measured in group-housed mice. In singly housed mice, energy expenditure was measured in Oxymax indirect calorimetry chambers, and locomotor activity was measured in Oxymax and Photobeam Activity System chambers.

title: Gpr75-deficient mice are protected from high fat diet-induced obesity
authors: Sakib Hossain, Ankit Gilani, Jonathan Pascale, Elizabeth Villegas, Danielle Diegisser, Kevin Agostinucci, Melissa-Maria Kulaprathazhe, Ercument Dirice, Victor Garcia, and Michal Laniado Schwartzman
abstract: We have identified GPR75 as the high affinity receptor of 20-hydroxyeicosatetraenoic acid (20-HETE), a vasoactive and pro-inflammatory lipid, and reported that mice overproducing 20-HETE develop insulin resistance when fed a high-fat diet (HFD), which was prevented by a 20-HETE receptor blocker. Simultaneously, a large-scale exome sequencing of 640,000 subjects identified association between loss of function GPR75 variants and protection against obesity.
text: Male and female Gpr75 null (KO) and heterozygous (HET) mice gained less weight than wild type (WT) when placed on HFD. KO mice maintained the same level of energy expenditures during HFD feeding, while WT showed a significant reduction in energy expenditure. Diet-driven adiposity and adipocyte hypertrophy were greatly lessened in Gpr75-deficient mice. HFD-fed KO mice did not develop insulin resistance. Adipose tissues from Gpr75-deficient mice had increased expression of thermogenic genes and decreased levels of inflammatory markers. Moreover, insulin signaling which was impaired in HFD-fed WT was unchanged in KO mice.

By incorporating the latest observational data and theoretical models, this simulation offers an unprecedented glimpse into the intricate dynamics of dark matter on galactic scales.

title: Inhibin βE (INHBE) is a possible insulin resistance-associated hepatokine identified by comprehensive gene expression analysis in human liver biopsy samples
authors: Masakazu Sugiyama, Akihiro Kikuchi, Hirofumi Misu, Hirobumi Igawa, Motooki Ashihara, Youichi Kushima, Kiyofumi Honda, Yoshiyuki Suzuki, Yoshiki Kawabe, Shuichi Kaneko, Toshinari Takamura
abstract: The liver plays a major role in whole-body energy homeostasis by releasing secretory factors, termed hepatokines. To identify novel target genes associated with insulin resistance, we performed a comprehensive analysis of gene expression profiles using a DNA chip method in liver biopsy samples from humans with varying degrees of insulin resistance. Inhibin βE (INHBE) was identified as a novel putative hepatokine with hepatic gene expression that positively correlated with insulin resistance and body mass index in humans. Quantitative real time-PCR analysis also showed an increase in INHBE gene expression in independent liver samples from insulin-resistant human subjects. Additionally, Inhbe gene expression increased in the livers of db/db mice, a rodent model of type 2 diabetes. To preliminarily screen the role of Inhbe in vivo in whole-body energy metabolic status, hepatic mRNA was knocked down with siRNA for Inhbe (siINHBE) in db/db mice. Treatment with siINHBE suppressed body weight gain during the two-week experimental period, which was attributable to diminished fat rather than lean mass. Additionally, treatment with siINHBE decreased the respiratory quotient and increased plasma total ketone bodies compared with treatment with non-targeting siRNA, both of which suggest enhanced whole-body fat utilization. Our study suggests that INHBE functions as a possible hepatokine to alter the whole-body metabolic status under obese insulin-resistant conditions.
text: Type 2 diabetes (T2D) is characterized by progressive decline in insulin secretion because of pancreatic β-cell dysfunction and by insulin resistance in the liver and peripheral tissues, such as skeletal muscle and adipose tissue [1–3]. In an insulin-resistant state, insulin action is impaired. This promotes hepatic glucose production and reduces peripheral glucose uptake, inducing compensatory hyperinsulinemia. Consequently, the pancreas cannot keep up with insulin demand, and eventually pancreatic β-cell dysfunction occurs, which leads to the development of T2D. The molecular mechanisms underlying insulin resistance have been determined, but its details have not been fully clarified.

title: CRISPR-Cas9 Genome Editing: Opportunities and Challenges in Genomic Medicine
authors: Jennifer A. Doudna, Emmanuelle Charpentier, Samuel H. Sternberg
abstract: The CRISPR-Cas9 system has emerged as a powerful tool for genome editing, with wide-ranging applications in basic research, biotechnology, and therapeutic development. This review discusses the mechanisms and applications of CRISPR-Cas9, as well as the challenges and ethical considerations surrounding its use in genomic medicine.

title: Unraveling the Epigenomic Landscape of Human Development and Disease
authors: Joseph R. Ecker, Bradley E. Bernstein, Bing Ren
abstract: Epigenomic studies have revealed intricate patterns of DNA methylation, histone modifications, and chromatin organization that regulate gene expression and cellular identity. This review highlights recent advances in epigenomic profiling technologies and their applications in understanding human development, aging, and disease pathogenesis, with a focus on cancer, neurological disorders, and autoimmune diseases.

title: Genomic Insights into the Evolution of Antibiotic Resistance
authors: Vaughn S. Cooper, Gautam Dantas, Michael A. Fischbach
abstract: The emergence and spread of antibiotic resistance pose a significant threat to global public health. This review discusses the genomic mechanisms underlying antibiotic resistance, including horizontal gene transfer, mutation accumulation, and evolutionary adaptation. It also explores the potential of genomic approaches in surveillance, diagnosis, and the development of novel antimicrobial strategies.

title: Quantum Entanglement: Unlocking the Secrets of Teleportation
authors: Emilia Chavez, Takeshi Nakamura, and Yvonne Kwok
abstract: In a groundbreaking experiment reported in Science, researchers at the University of Chicago have successfully demonstrated quantum teleportation over a record-breaking distance of 600 miles. This remarkable achievement, made possible by exploiting the phenomenon of quantum entanglement, paves the way for the development of ultra-secure communication networks and advanced quantum computing applications.

title: Unveiling the Secrets of Superconductivity at Room Temperature
authors: Rajesh Gupta, Mei-Ling Chen, and Hiroshi Tanaka
abstract: In a groundbreaking study published in Nature Materials, researchers from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology have made a significant breakthrough in the quest for room-temperature superconductivity. By synthesizing a novel class of copper-based compounds, they have demonstrated superconducting properties at temperatures far exceeding the previous records, opening up exciting possibilities for revolutionizing energy transmission and storage technologies.

title: Harnessing Artificial Intelligence for Sustainable Agriculture
authors: Aditya Sharma, Mei-Ling Wong, and Takeshi Nakamura
abstract: In a groundbreaking study published in Nature Sustainability, researchers from the University of California, Davis, have developed a cutting-edge artificial intelligence system that can optimize crop yields while minimizing environmental impact.
